subject: English
passage: The Alchemist is a 1610 play by Ben Jonson, originally written in English. At the time, self-styled alchemists circulated through London claiming they could transmute base metals into gold and produce miraculous elixirs, often charging desperate or ambitious clients large sums for these promised services. In the play, Jonson satirizes alchemists as knowingly deceiving their clients while exploiting their greed for personal profit, as seen when the character ______
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses a quotation from The Alchemist to illustrate the claim?

choices.A: Subtle, an alchemist, describes his laboratory work to a client, saying, "The fire, sir, must be kept at one even heat, lest the calcination prove imperfect and the spirits flee before their time."
choices.B: Mammon, a wealthy client, declares his eagerness to acquire the philosopher's stone, exclaiming, "This day, I shall be rich; the elixir is mine, and with it all the wonders of the world!"
choices.C: Subtle, an alchemist, greets a new visitor at the door, saying, "Welcome, sir; pray, what business brings you hither, and what service may we render you in our humble laboratory?"
choices.D: Subtle, an alchemist, says to his partner Face after a client has left, "Mark how the fellow's purse opens at the very mention of gold; we need only feed his hopes a little longer, and the whole estate shall pour itself into our coffers."

explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. The quotation shows Subtle, an alchemist, speaking privately to his partner about a client whose 'purse opens at the very mention of gold,' indicating that Subtle is consciously playing on the client's greed. Subtle further plans to 'feed his hopes a little longer' so that 'the whole estate' will flow into their pockets — an explicit acknowledgment that the alchemist is deceiving the client in order to extract profit. This quotation captures both components of the claim: knowing deception and exploitation of the client's greed for personal gain.

Why B is incorrect:

Choice B is incorrect. Although the quotation vividly conveys Mammon's greed for wealth and miraculous transformation, it portrays the client's perspective rather than the alchemist's actions. It does not show the alchemist deceiving anyone or deliberately exploiting that greed for profit, so it fails to illustrate the satirical claim about how Jonson depicts the alchemists themselves.
